subject: biology
title: Interacting limiting factors and the inverse square law
key_idea: (Higher tier) Several limiting factors act together, and any one of them may be the one limiting photosynthesis. Light intensity falls with the square of the distance from the source. Greenhouse growers add heat, light or carbon dioxide only while the extra profit pays for the cost.

blocks.text: (Higher tier) Light, carbon dioxide and temperature all act at once. This section covers how to decide which one is limiting from a graph.

items: Any one of the factors may be the factor that limits photosynthesis.
The factor in shortest supply limits the rate.
Increasing a factor that is not limiting makes no difference to the rate.
Once the limiting factor is increased, another factor may become the limiting one.

diagram.alt: Three curves of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity. All rise together at low light intensity. Each then levels off at its own height: lowest with low carbon dioxide, higher with high carbon dioxide, and highest with high carbon dioxide and a higher temperature.

blocks.text: Reading a graph with more than one factor

items.text: The factor on the x axis (light intensity) is the limiting factor.
Light is no longer limiting. Another factor, shown by the label on the line, is limiting.
A line that levels off higher has had the limiting factor increased, for example more carbon dioxide.

items: The factor in shortest supply is the limiting factor.
On a flat part of the graph, light is not limiting. Another factor is.

sections.heading: The inverse square law for light (Higher tier)

blocks.text: (Higher tier) Light spreads out as it travels, so a plant further from a lamp receives much less light.

blocks.label: Inverse square law
where: d is the distance from the light source, in cm

items: Light intensity is **inversely proportional** to the **square** of the distance.
Double the distance and the light intensity is a quarter.
When light is the limiting factor, the rate of photosynthesis is directly proportional to light intensity.

blocks.text: Move the slider to see how quickly the light intensity falls.

diagram.alt: Change the distance from the lamp. The light intensity, calculated as 1 divided by distance squared, falls quickly as the distance increases.

items.text: The distance doubled and the intensity fell to a quarter.

items: Doubling the distance quarters the light intensity.
Always square the distance before you divide.

blocks.text: (Higher tier) Growers can control the conditions in a greenhouse, but each change costs money.

items: They can add heat, light or carbon dioxide to increase the rate of photosynthesis.
A faster rate makes more glucose, so plants grow faster and make more protein and cellulose.
Heating, lighting and extra carbon dioxide all cost money.
It is only worth adding one if the extra sales cover its cost.
Adding more of a factor that is not limiting wastes money.
Increase the limiting factor to raise the rate.
Stop when the extra cost is more than the extra profit.

checks.q: A graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity levels off. Explain what this shows.
checks.a: Light intensity is no longer the limiting factor. Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, is limiting the rate.

checks.q: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm away from a plant. Explain what happens to the light intensity. Include a calculation.
checks.a: 1 ÷ 10² = 0.01 and 1 ÷ 20² = 0.0025. The distance doubled, so the light intensity is a quarter.

checks.q: Why might a grower not heat a greenhouse as much as possible?
checks.a: Heating costs money. The extra cost might be more than the extra sale price of the crop, so profit would not increase.

exam_phrases: evidence of squaring for two distances that double: 25 and 100
calculate 1/d² for two distances that double: 0.04 and 0.01
(therefore as distance doubles) light intensity is quartered
there is a cost for heating the greenhouse
there is a cost for increasing the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
the additional costs might exceed the (additional) sale price / profit

mistakes.wrong: When the distance doubles, the light intensity halves.
mistakes.right: Intensity is proportional to 1 ÷ d². Doubling the distance (5 cm to 10 cm) changes 1 ÷ 25 = 0.04 to 1 ÷ 100 = 0.01, so the intensity is quartered.

mistakes.wrong: The extra heating costs would reduce the farmer's profits.
mistakes.right: "Additional costs would reduce profits" on its own is ignored. Name the costs, such as heating, lighting or carbon dioxide, and say the extra costs might be more than the extra sale price.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis. The student placed pondweed at 5 cm, 10 cm and 20 cm from a light source.

Light intensity can be calculated using the inverse square law: I ∝ 1/d², where I is light intensity and d is the distance of the pondweed from the light source.

Explain how light intensity changes as the distance of the pondweed from the light source is doubled.

You must include calculations in your answer.
answer_points: Squaring two distances that double: 5² = 25 and 10² = 100 (or 10² = 100 and 20² = 400).
Calculating 1/d² for those distances: 1/25 = 0.04 and 1/100 = 0.01 (or 0.01 and 0.0025).
Therefore, as the distance doubles, the light intensity is quartered.
worked_example.tip: Use two distances where one is double the other. Two marks are available for the calculations even without working.

mistakes.right: The distance must be squared first: 25² = 625, so the light intensity is 1 ÷ 625 = 0.0016 arbitrary units.

mistakes.wrong: I wrote down 0.0016 but did not give the equation.
mistakes.right: The question asks for the equation to be included. Write light intensity ∝ 1/d² and show 1 ÷ 25² as well as the answer.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the photosynthesis of pondweed. A light source was placed at different distances from the pondweed. The light intensity was calculated using the inverse square law for photosynthesis.

The light intensity was 0.04 arbitrary units at 5 cm, 0.01 at 10 cm, 0.0044 at 15 cm and 0.0025 at 20 cm.

Calculate the light intensity at a distance of 25 cm from the lamp.

Include the equation for the inverse square law in your answer.
worked_example.tip: A correct answer with no working gets full marks, but showing the equation and the square protects your marks.

exam_phrases: molecules move faster / increased kinetic energy
increased rate of collisions between enzymes and substrates
high temperature (above 37 °C) will stop / reduce the rate of photosynthesis
enzymes / structural proteins may start to denature

mistakes.wrong: Increasing the temperature from 15 °C to 40 °C always makes photosynthesis faster.
mistakes.right: The rate rises because of more kinetic energy and more enzyme-substrate collisions. At high temperatures (above 37 °C) the rate stops or falls, because enzymes may start to denature.

mistakes.wrong: Higher temperature only changes the rate of photosynthesis.
mistakes.right: Temperature affects other plant processes too. Increased temperature will also increase respiration, transpiration or water uptake, and any of these can earn the mark.

worked_example.question:
Light is one environmental factor that affects plants.

Explain how increasing the temperature from 15 °C to 40 °C can affect plants.
answer_points: Increased temperature will increase photosynthesis (or respiration, transpiration or water uptake).
Molecules move faster / have increased kinetic energy.
There is an increased rate of collisions between enzymes and substrates (more enzyme-substrate complexes form).
High temperatures (above 37 °C) will stop or reduce the rate of photosynthesis or respiration.
Any three of these points score.
worked_example.tip: Give the rise with its reason, and say what happens at the highest temperatures.
